title: Mahabali, the asura devotee
hookLine: a festival song about a king so good that the gods grew worried
carry: devotion counts, not the side you're born on
tomorrow: Bali's teacher says: take back your word. will he?

lines: A SONG ABOUT A GOOD KING
A KING FROM THE OTHER SIDE
cards: When Maveli ruled the land, everyone was alike. That's the opening, in paraphrase, of a folk song sung in Kerala at Onam. It goes on: there was no theft and no cheating, not even a small lie.
Nobody was in trouble, and nobody was afraid. It sounds like a children's daydream. But the king in the song isn't a god.
He's an asura, from the side of the stories usually cast as the gods' rivals. And he was so good at being king that heaven itself got nervous.

teach.b: Year one gave you Onam: a king's yearly homecoming. Here is the king. His name is Bali, and Kerala calls him Mahabali, great Bali, or Maveli for short.
His story is told in the Bhagavata Purana. He's the grandson of Prahlada, the boy devotee who held to Vishnu through every danger.
Bali is generous, devout and strong, and with the help of his teacher Shukra, he wins the three worlds, heaven included. The gods are pushed out. Their mother, Aditi, grieves for them and prays.
And notice what the text does not say. It never calls Bali cruel. His problem isn't wickedness.

teach.h: A GOOD KING ON A THRONE NOT HIS
teach.b: A good man is sitting on a throne that isn't his. Vishnu answers Aditi's prayer by being born as her son, Vamana, a small brahmin boy. He walks to Bali's great sacrifice, where the king is giving gifts to anyone who asks.
Bali welcomes him warmly: ask for anything.
And the boy asks only for as much ground as he can cover in three of his own steps. Bali calls it a child's request. Now the teaching under the story.
Hindu stories don't split the world into a good team and a bad team.
Asuras are usually the gods' rivals, yet the Bhagavata names Bali, and his grandfather Prahlada, among its twelve mahajanas, the great ones who truly know the path of devotion.
What makes someone great is devotion and dharma, not the side they were born on. That's why a whole festival in Kerala can long for an asura king.

how: At Onam, families in Kerala remember Mahabali's reign with songs, flower designs at the door and a shared feast, and the Bhagavata Purana's account of Bali and Vamana is retold.

games.q: what does “kerala's onam and ayyappa” mean?
o: a boat race for Shiva, and a hermit of the hills
a festival for a good king, and a god of a forest hill
a feast for a river goddess, and a king of the sea

games.q: the king and the boy — tap the pairs.
p: Vishnu as a small brahmin boy

s: in the Bhagavata Purana, Bali's problem is that he is cruel
the text doesn't call him cruel: he's generous and devout, but the throne of heaven isn't his.
the Onam song remembers a land with no theft and no lies
the folk song says that when Maveli ruled, everyone was alike, with no cheating, not even a small lie.
the Bhagavata names Bali, an asura, among its twelve great devotees
with his grandfather Prahlada, Bali is one of the twelve mahajanas, the great ones who know the path of devotion.

games.q: at an Onam lunch, a cousin says: 'asuras are the bad guys, so why welcome one?' by the Bhagavata, what fits?
o: Bali was an asura and a great devotee: goodness isn't decided by sides.
asuras are always villains; Kerala just likes the story.
Bali was secretly a god all along, so he doesn't count.
games.why: the Bhagavata never calls Bali cruel, and names him with Prahlada among its twelve great devotees, the mahajanas.

practice: Bring to mind someone you'd usually put on the other side: another school, another team, another way of seeing the world. Hold them for a minute the way the Bhagavata holds Bali, as someone whose goodness might be real.
Rest with the breath. If you pray, you can say Om Namo Narayanaya softly, a prayer to Vishnu many Hindus say, the god both Prahlada and Bali loved.

wordCard.voice: Kerala's Onam and Ayyappa. Today, Onam's beginning: Mahabali, the asura king counted among the great devotees, and the small boy who asked him for three steps of ground. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Vamana, the small brahmin boy Vishnu becomes in the story of Bali.

carryVoice: Your line: devotion counts, not the side you're born on. Bali was an asura, and one of the great devotees. Tomorrow, the three steps.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 8.15–8.19 (Bali wins the three worlds; Aditi's grief; Vamana's birth and request for three steps)
